Lab 1

title: Lab #1
text:
Today
Three hours, three parts:

Set up a development environment — compiler, terminal, editor. On Windows: WSL 2, a real Linux inside Windows.
Introduction to C++ (part I) — the object oriented paradigm: encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance. From C to C++ with three short examples.
Task: a vector class from scratch — pvector.hpp and its main in pvector.cpp: constructors and destructor, overloading of =, + and -, arguments passed by reference, this, const methods, using and constexpr.

pvector is the first brick of the simulation codes (Monte Carlo and Molecular Dynamics) we will write in the next labs: positions, velocities and forces of the particles will all be pvectors.

In this course we compile from the terminal, with one command: you see exactly what happens, and it works the same way everywhere.
Any editor is fine (VS Code, vim, emacs, …): what matters is to have a C++ compiler that supports at least C++17.
On Windows we do not use MinGW or Visual Studio: with WSL you get the same environment as on a Linux machine (and later the same packages, e.g. for the molgl visualizer).

title: Lab #1
text:
Windows: what is WSL 2
WSL = Windows Subsystem for Linux. Version 2 runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight virtual machine managed by Windows:

you get a Linux distribution (Ubuntu by default) with its terminal, apt, g++, make, gdb, …
no dual boot, no VirtualBox: Ubuntu is an app, it starts in a few seconds;
Linux and Windows see each other’s files;
graphical Linux programs open their windows on the Windows desktop (WSLg).

Requirements: Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later, and hardware virtualization enabled (it usually is on recent laptops).

title: Lab #1
text:
Installing WSL 2

Open PowerShell as administrator (right click on Start → Terminal (Admin)).
Run
wsl --install
It enables the required Windows features, installs WSL 2 and Ubuntu.
Restart Windows.
Open the Ubuntu app (Start menu). The first time it asks for a UNIX username and password: choose them and remember the password, it is the one sudo will ask for. While you type it nothing is shown: that is normal.
Check, from PowerShell:
wsl -l -v          # NAME: Ubuntu   STATE: Running   VERSION: 2

title: Lab #1
text:
If something goes wrong

VERSION is 1 → wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2, and for the future wsl --set-default-version 2.
Error about virtualization (e.g. 0x80370102) → enable it in the BIOS/UEFI (Intel VT-x or AMD-V / SVM), then retry.
Older Windows 10, wsl --install only prints the help → enable the two features by hand, from an administrator PowerShell, then restart and install Ubuntu from the Microsoft Store:
dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux /all /norestart
dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:VirtualMachinePlatform /all /norestart
Keep WSL up to date: wsl --update; general status: wsl --status.

title: Lab #1
text:
Inside Ubuntu: the compiler
From the Ubuntu terminal (the same commands on a native Ubuntu/Debian machine):
sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential gdb    # g++, gcc, make, the C/C++ headers, the debugger
g++ --version                           # check
On macOS the compiler comes with the Xcode command line tools:
xcode-select --install
g++ --version        # it prints "Apple clang ...": fine, g++ is an alias of clang++
On Fedora: sudo dnf install gcc-c++ make gdb.
Later in the course we will also install the libraries for molgl, the program we use to look at the configurations (freeglut, libpng): not today.

title: Lab #1
section: WSL: where to keep your files
text:
WSL: where to keep your files

Work in your Linux home, e.g. ~/csm/lab01, not on the Windows disk /mnt/c/...: compiling and running from /mnt/c is much slower.
From Linux, the Windows disk is under /mnt/c. To copy the lab files you downloaded with the browser:
mkdir -p ~/csm/lab01
cp /mnt/c/Users/<your Windows user>/Downloads/pvector.* ~/csm/lab01/
From Windows, the Linux files are in the Linux entry of File Explorer, or at \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\<your Linux user>.
Quick trick: explorer.exe . opens the current Linux folder in File Explorer.

title: Lab #1
section: The editor: VS Code with WSL
text:
The editor: VS Code with WSL
If you do not have a favourite editor, use Visual Studio Code (free, all systems):

Install it on Windows (not inside Ubuntu), then add the WSL extension (Microsoft).
From the Ubuntu terminal, inside your project folder:
cd ~/csm/lab01
code .
The first time it installs its server inside Linux; the window then works directly on the Linux files (bottom left: WSL: Ubuntu).
Install the C/C++ extension (Microsoft) in WSL: syntax highlighting, completion, errors while you type.
Terminal → New Terminal opens a Linux terminal inside VS Code: compile there.

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Object oriented (OO) paradigm
Key concepts
Encapsulation

Separate implementation from interface.
Attributes (data members) and methods (functions) can be public (→ interface) or private (→ implementation, hidden to user).
No need to know/remember internals of all objects.







Methods/functions act on objects and return objects (as an operator does) ⇓



Polymorphism — functions/methods can behave differently depending on the objects they act on: function overloading, operator overloading (e.g. + - / *), pointers.
Example: \(a + b\) (scalars) or \(\vec a + \vec b\) (vectors): operator “+” overloading.
Inheritance — in OO paradigm we have custom types called classes and we can enrich a class with more attributes and methods from base one.

title: Lab #1
text:
Example: custom types
From a non OO language (C) to an OO language (C++)

C language can be thought as a subset of C++.
In C you have objects (variables) of several different types such as char, int, float, double and operators that act on them (such as ++, --, +, *, etc.).
C++ introduces custom types (similar to struct) called “classes” and it allows operators and methods to act on them.








Note


In C you had struct which could embed attributes but not methods. Hence classes can be also thought as a generalization of “struct”.

title: Lab #1
text:
Instantiation
int, double, float ← fundamental types of C language.
If one writes
double d;   // double: type/class    d: instance of class "double", i.e. an OBJECT
Assume you have a custom type, i.e. a class, called vector which represents a vector. You can instantiate it as follows:
vector v;   // v is an instance of this class, i.e. an object
If we have
vector a, b, c;
and we “overloaded” the operators = and +, we can write
c = a + b;

title: Lab #1
section: The goal of the first labs
text:
The goal of the first labs
Similarly we can overload other operators such as ==, ++, --, *, /, *=, etc.
And this is precisely the goal of the first part of these hands-on classes, i.e.






learn how to write your own class to handle vectors and matrices for computations.

text:
Example 2: using the class
ex2_a_cpp_class.cpp:
#include "./ex2_a_cpp_class.hpp"
int main(void)
{
  myclass C;   // a new type! the constructor runs here
  C.show();
}              // C goes out of scope here: the destructor runs
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -o ex2 ex2_a_cpp_class.cpp && ./ex2
Object created
no!
Hallo World 2
Object destroyed

We never call constructor and destructor explicitly: the compiler does it, when the object is born and when it dies.
The class is in a header (.hpp), the main in a .cpp that #includes it: we compile only the .cpp.

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
section: Example N1: a first vector class

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Constructors and destructor
pvector()  { ... }   // void constructor: pvector P;
~pvector() { ... }   // destructor

The void constructor should leave the vector in a known state: all components set to zero. (A local double v[3] in C contains garbage!)
The destructor has nothing to do here: v is a fixed-size array, it disappears with the object. Leave it empty (we will need it when we allocate memory dynamically).

Constructor overloading: a class can have several constructors, which differ by their arguments. We want to write
pvector V = {1.0, 2.0, 3.0};    // V = (1,2,3)
pvector W = {4.0, 5.0};         // W = (4,5,0): missing components are zero
Not in the skeleton: you add it.

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Arguments passed by reference
void twice_val(int x)  { x = 2*x; }   // by value: x is a COPY, the caller sees nothing
void twice_ref(int &x) { x = 2*x; }   // by reference: x is an alias of the argument

int a = 3;
twice_val(a);   // a is still 3
twice_ref(a);   // a is now 6
In the class all the vector arguments are passed as const pvector&:
pvector operator+(const pvector& V2) const

&: no copy of the object (for a vector of 3 doubles it is cheap, but think of a configuration of \(10^5\) particles…).
const: the method promises not to modify V2; the compiler enforces it.
Inside a method of pvector you can read the private members of another pvector: V2.v[i] is legal. Access is per class, not per object.

title: Lab #1
text:
operator= and this
The one method already implemented in the skeleton:
1pvector& operator=(const pvector& V2)   // A = B  is  A.operator=(B)
  {
    for (int i=0; i < NT; i++)
      v[i] = V2.v[i];                   // v[i] is A's, V2.v[i] is B's
2    return (*this);
  }

1

A = B is just a nicer way to write the method call A.operator=(B): A is the object the method acts on, B the argument.

2

this is the address of the object the method has been called on (A); *this is the object itself. v[i] is a shorthand for (*this).v[i].



It returns a reference to A itself (pvector&), not a copy: so A = B = C; works, as for double — it is A = (B = C).
It is not const: it changes the object.

title: Lab #1
text:
sum(), operator+ and operator-
pvector sum(const pvector &V2) const      // C = A.sum(B)
pvector operator+(const pvector& V2) const // C = A + B   is   C = A.operator+(B)
pvector operator-(const pvector& V2) const // C = A - B
Recipe, the same for the three:

create a local vector VT;
fill it component by component, using v[i] (of A) and V2.v[i] (of B);
return VT;


They are const: A + B must change neither A nor B.
They return by value (pvector, not pvector&): VT is a local object, destroyed when the method ends. A reference to it would point to a dead object (g++ warns: reference to local variable returned).
sum() and operator+ do the same thing: the operator is just nicer to read. Once one is written, the other can call it.

title: Lab #1
text:
get() and set()
ntype get(int i) const          // returns the i-th component
ntype set(int i, ntype val)     // sets the i-th component to val

get is const, set is not: why?
set in the skeleton returns an ntype: return val (or change it to void, as in myvec).
Components are numbered from 0 to NT-1, as in C. Nothing checks the index: get(3) reads outside the array (undefined behaviour).








Compile with -Wall while you work


The empty bodies of the skeleton compile: a method that should return a value and has no return is accepted, and its result is garbage (undefined behaviour). With -Wall the compiler tells you: warning: no return statement in function returning non-void [-Wreturn-type].

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Compile, run, compare
cd ~/csm/lab01
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -o pvector pvector.cpp
./pvector
Expected output:
A=(1,2,3)
D=(4,5,0)
A+B=(1.5,1,5)
A-B=(0.5,3,1)
A.sum(B)=(1.5,1,5)
B(0)=10
E=(1,2,3)
PC=(0.2,0.3,0.4)

No warnings with -Wall: if there are, read them — they are usually a bug.
Change NT to 2 and ntype to float: everything must still compile and run.

title: Lab #1
text:
Classic pitfalls

; after the class: class pvector { ... }; — without it the error appears in the next line, often in another file.
pvector P(); is not an object: it declares a function P returning a pvector. Write pvector P; (or pvector P{};).
Returning a reference to a local object in operator+: it compiles (with a warning) and gives garbage.
Missing const on show() or get(): then they cannot be called on a const pvector, nor on an argument const pvector& V2.
Missing return in a non-void method: see -Wall.
Header guard: #ifndef _PVECTOR_ / #define _PVECTOR_ / ... #endif stops the class from being defined twice when the header is included more than once.
